title: Holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3)
hookLine: congregations rise on their toes, like angels, at "Holy, holy, holy"

cards: Three words, and a room full of people leaves the floor. The leader is repeating the Amidah out loud. The room has been still.
Then, at those words, people lift up on their toes. Old men in suits, kids in sneakers, a woman holding a toddler on her hip: up, down, up, down, up, down.
For a second the whole congregation bobs like a field in the wind. It looks almost playful. It comes from a vision that left a prophet crying out that he was undone.

teach.b: The scene is Isaiah, chapter six. The prophet sees the Lord on a high throne, the hem of the robe filling the Temple, and seraphim standing above.
In the old Jewish translation: "And one called unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory."

teach.h: KADOSH: SET APART, YET FILLING ALL.
teach.b: Kadosh, kadosh, kadosh. Jewish teachers often hear in kadosh the sense of set apart, other, not ordinary. Yet the second half says this utterly other God fills the whole earth.
Far and near in one sentence. The Kedushah, sanctification, is the leader's expanded version of the Amidah's third blessing.
It weaves together three verses: Isaiah's holy, holy, holy; Ezekiel's line, "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from His place"; and a line from Psalm 146, the Lord will reign forever.

teach.h: THREE VERSES, CALLED BACK AND FORTH.
teach.b: The congregation calls out the verses and the leader answers, back and forth, the way the seraphim called one to another.
It's said only with a minyan, a quorum of ten, because the Talmud treats the public sanctifying of God's name as needing a community.
Alone, the blessing is shorter: You are holy. And the toes?
Many people rise on each holy, a custom recorded in the codes of Jewish law, often explained as reaching upward toward the angels, whose feet, you heard last week, are straight.
For three words, a room full of ordinary people tries to stand the way angels stand.

how: During the leader's repetition of the Amidah, with a minyan present, the congregation and leader recite the Kedushah in call and response; many people stand with feet together and rise on their toes at each kadosh and at the following verses.

o: a blessing said before reading the Torah
the holy, holy, holy said aloud with a minyan
the blessing over wine that begins Shabbat

games.q: inside the Kedushah — tap the pairs.
p: blessed be the glory from His place

s: the Kedushah can be said by one person praying alone
it needs a minyan; alone, the blessing is the shorter you are holy.
the call and answer echoes the seraphim calling to one another
one called unto another: the congregation and leader answer back and forth.
kadosh means only nice or good
Jewish teachers read kadosh as set apart, other than ordinary.

games.q: you're praying the Amidah at home, alone. you reach the third blessing. what do you say?
o: the full Kedushah with all three verses.
the shorter blessing: You are holy.
games.why: the Kedushah's call and answer is for a minyan. alone, you say the short third blessing, atah kadosh.

practice: If you can stand, stand with your feet together, breathe in, and rise slowly onto your toes, hold for a second, and come back down. Notice the tiny wobble, and how high you actually get, which is not very; that's part of it.
If you pray, you can say the three words as you rise; if not, let the rising itself say something about reaching toward what's bigger than you.

wordCard.voice: Kedushah. Sanctification. The call and answer of holy, holy, holy in the leader's Amidah, said with a minyan, on your toes.

orig.note: Hebrew: holy, holy, holy. Isaiah 6:3, the heart of the Kedushah.

carryVoice: Your line: feet together, rising. Far and near, in one sentence. Day five hundred eighty, done.
